CTS Exam Guide · Part IV

Implementing AV Solutions

Part IV is where the design becomes real: physically installing the system, verifying it performs to spec and handing it over to trained users, and managing the whole project so it lands on time and on budget. These three chapters cover the build-and-deliver phase of AV work.

ChapterTopicApprox. Exam Weight
Ch 17Integrating AV solutions (installation)~10% (~10 questions)
Ch 18Operating AV solutions (verification & handover)~9% (~9 questions)
Ch 19Managing an AV project~8% (~8 questions)
🎯 Exam Tip

Part IV rewards process and sequence knowledge: what gets tested/terminated first, the right order to power a system up and down, when AV work slots into the construction schedule, and which document does which job. When two answers seem right, favor the one that's safer, earlier in the correct sequence, or properly coordinated with other trades.

CHAPTER 17Integrating AV Solutions

The hands-on installation chapter: reading the design docs, terminating cable, building racks, pulling cable, mounting heavy gear safely, wiring and configuring control systems and networks, and setting up temporary event systems.

Preparing for the Install & Job-Site Safety

Good installation starts before you reach the site. Know each project's priority, review the documentation with the sales rep, designer, or project manager, understand your scope and how success is measured, know which sites you're at each day, and study the facility and system drawings first. Confirm you have the tools, consumables, and manuals you need — and on arrival, open and inspect every box, checking for damage and powering on each device to confirm it works before you install it.

🎯 Exam Tip

Safety is always the primary concern on a job site. The safety framework carries over from Chapter 12: comply with the AHJ and all applicable codes, wear the required PPE (hard hats, protected-toe footwear, gloves, hearing and eye protection), and use approved ladders and fall protection when needed.

Cable Termination

📌 Key Term

Cable termination — establishing the connection at each end of a cable by selecting the right cable and connector and using the proper tools and method. Poor terminations are the single most prevalent problem in electronic systems — expensive to find after the build because the faults are often intermittent. A CTS professional must be an expert at terminating cable.

Cable stripping removes the jacket (and sometimes shield/insulation) to reveal the conductor. Strip with a tool matched to the specific cable and connector — improper stripping distorts the insulation and alters the cable's impedance. Remove the outer jacket first without disturbing the wires beneath.

Termination methods

MethodHow it worksTypical use
Direct-connection (screw-down)Wire wraps a screw, or a crimped spade lug is screwed down; barrier strips, utility blocks, screw terminalsPermanent connections — loudspeakers, relay switches, points of demarcation
CompressionA captive-screw connector presses a flat plate onto the wire to hold itPermanent screw-clamp terminations
SolderingJoins metal with heat and a metallic alloyXLR, phono/RCA, phone (6.5mm), 3.5mm TRS connectors
CrimpingA hand tool applies pressure to attach the connector — permanentMany pin/lug connectors
Linear-compressionCable inserted into a special connector, then compressed lengthwise — permanentBNC connectors for video/RF on coax
Insulation-displacement (IDC)Wire pushed through a slot; a metal strip cuts the insulation and grabs the conductor8P8C / RJ-45 modular connectors (Cat cable)
📌 Key Term

Connector cheat sheet: XLR = balanced audio, 3–7 pins, soldered. RCA/phono = unbalanced audio & legacy composite video. Phone 6.5mm (¼") = line-level audio, TS or TRS. 3.5mm (⅛") TRS = stereo audio from computers/multimedia. BNC = video/RF on coax, linear compression. 8P8C / RJ-45 = network cable, insulation displacement.

Evaluating & testing terminations

Test every termination immediately after making it — far cheaper than after the whole system is built. Visually inspect for stray wires (short-circuit risk), correct wires at the correct pins, excessive or insufficient solder, and sharp protrusions or foreign matter. Then test electrically: a multimeter checks continuity and shorts for many termination types; an 8P8C modular connector has a dedicated pin-to-pin continuity tester.

⚠ Watch Out

To confirm a termination is actually passing signal, the correct check is a continuity test — not a voltage, isolation, or "signal sweep" test. This is a common exam distractor.

T568A vs. T568B Pin-Out

⚠ Watch Out

Pick one standard and use it at both ends throughout a job. A cable terminated T568A at one end and T568B at the other is a crossover cable — which is occasionally what you want, and much more often the reason a link will not come up.

Rack Building

📌 Key Term

Equipment rack — the skeletal framework where system components are housed, arranged, and interconnected. Space is measured in rack units (RU). Rack building is three distinct tasks: building the rack (frame, shelves, cable management, power), installing the equipment, and wiring the hardware together.

Don't mount equipment haphazardly. Layout considerations: how much heat each device emits and how it will be managed, the signal types on interconnecting cables, which devices need user access, and weight distribution. The designer usually provides a rack-elevation drawing showing each device's position and RU count.

Layout
Ergonomics

User-interface gear (patch fields, EQs, media players) goes within easy reach; rarely-accessed gear at top or bottom. For accessibility, interactive features belong between 380–1,220 mm (15–48 in) above the floor — about 840 mm (33 in) of usable space per rack.

Layout
Weight distribution

Avoid top-heavy racks. In a free-standing rack, heavy components go at the bottom or it can tip. Heavy 1–2 RU gear may need rear rails to counter front-panel torque.

Layout
RF & IR reception

A metal rack shields antennas — mount RF receiver antennas facing forward or away from the rack; IR needs line of sight or a relay emitter. A metal rack door blocks RF/IR; a transparent acrylic door generally doesn't.

Heat loads: three cooling methods

MethodHow it works
ConvectionPassive — hot air rises out top vents, cool air enters at the bottom. Only for racks producing relatively little heat.
EvacuationFans draw hot air out (usually top vents); cool air is passively pulled in from the bottom.
Forced airThe opposite of evacuation — fans push cool/chilled air in from below; hot air exhausts through top vents.

Also separate high-heat gear, place the hottest equipment near the top, and use vented and blank panels to manage airflow — never leave rack spaces empty, as gaps disrupt cooling.

📌 Key Term

Signal separation — grouping equipment and cables in a rack by function and signal type to reduce crosstalk from electromagnetic interference (EMI). A rack may carry microphone-level signals (~0.001 V) alongside loudspeaker-level signals (~30 V); physical separation preserves the weak signals. This principle repeats when bundling cables for pulling.

Rack assembly is best done in the workshop. Key steps: assemble the rack, install mechanical accessories (power, grounding, cable management, casters, fans), record serial numbers before loading (they're hard to reach later), attach mounting ears, load per the elevation drawing (a common best practice is laying the rack on its back to insert gear from above), fill all spaces, then wire — selecting correct cables, avoiding tight bends, maximizing signal separation, keeping cable lengths near-minimum, terminating, labeling, tying off, testing continuity, and finally installing AC power and grounding. A finished rack should look neat inside and out.

Cable Handling & Pulling

Technicians run cable from source to destination through raceways — ducts, conduit, junction and pull boxes, cable trays, or ladders. Typically electricians install the support/enclosure hardware; AV techs pull cable through it.

📌 Key Term

Junction box = installed at the ends of conduit runs. Pull box = installed at intermediate points for access to pull cable. Specify a pull box every 30 m (100 ft) of conduit, or after 180° of total bend.

Raceways & conduit types

A raceway is an enclosed channel for wires and cables (conduits, ducts; plus cable trays, ladders, wireways, troughs). Conduit is a circular tube housing cable. PVC conduit gives no EMI protection, so don't use it for unshielded AV cable; grounded metal conduit shields against incoming and outgoing EMI.

Metal conduitCharacter
EMT (electrical metallic tubing)"Thinwall" — most popular; not for high-abuse environments like gym or stage floors
Flexible metal ("flex")For movable equipment — e.g., a document camera on a cart pulled from a wall
Rigid metal (RMC / "rigid")Heaviest, best physical protection; prethreaded; needs elbow couplers since it can't be bent on-site
📐 Spec

Conduit fill / permissible area (max cross-sectional area cables may occupy; varies by jurisdiction): 1 cable = 53% · 2 cables = 31% · 3 cables = 40%. Sum each cable's cross-sectional area and compare to the conduit's permissible area to see if the run fits.

Ducts, troughs, cable trays, and ladders suit many cables running to similar places. A cable tray is rigid noncombustible support; troughs/wireways/cable ducts are sheet-metal wells with covers, sometimes internally partitioned for EMI separation between signal types.

Preparing & pulling

Plan which cables share which conduit before pulling (they're pulled together). Check cable stock against the drawings — a cable riser drawing shows all device interconnections. On site, locate the floor/ceiling/wall boxes (ceiling boxes may hide above tiles; display boxes sit ~1800 mm / 70 in up; speakers higher) and be careful not to confuse a fire-alarm or network box for your location.

📌 Key Term

Pull-through bundle (or cable snout) — multiple cables held with a constricting metal grip or bundled with tape and a pull string, so they pull as one. Bundle only one signal type per bundle, and above all keep microphone cables separate — their signal level is so low they're the most susceptible to interference.

Signal-separation grouping categories: microphone · line-level audio & communication · video · control & data · RF · loudspeaker · AC power · dimmed lighting. Label cables before installation, then apply permanent labels after terminating.

📌 Key Term

Draw wire / fish tape — a long flexible metal or fiberglass tape used to pull cable through conduit: fish it in from the far end, attach a pull string or the cable, and pull through. Pulling tension is the force applied — too much stretches conductors and changes their electrical properties (critical for twisted-pair). Bend radius is how tightly a cable can bend before its properties change; the tightest safe radius is about 4× the cable diameter (most critical for twisted-pair, fiber, and coax).

⚠ Watch Out

Pulling best-practices worth remembering: pull from spools rather than cutting to length; cross cables at 90° to minimize crosstalk; run low-level signals by the most direct route; feed cable in straight without twisting; don't pull too fast (it damages jackets); and if a cable wrinkles, bulges, or distorts, it has bent too far — discard it. Coordinate to pull plenum cable after ducts/supports but before ceiling tiles.

Mounting AV Components

Installers permanently mount displays, projectors, screens, and loudspeakers to walls and overhead structures — often above audiences, and flat panels can exceed 50 kg (110 lb), so safe mounting is critical. The mounting location and approach usually come from the design documents; if in doubt about safety, consult a professional engineer.

📌 Key Term

Load limit — the weight at which a mounting system structurally fails. The safe working load (SWL) / working load limit (WLL) must never be exceeded, and it includes the equipment plus all mounting hardware. Standards bodies (ISO, DIN, ASTM, SAE) rate hardware strength.

📐 Spec

Safety factor = 5. Design the mount to support five times the equipment weight. A 50 kg (110 lb) loudspeaker + hardware → use a mount rated for 250 kg (550 lb). (Also called the design factor, load factor, or safety ratio.)

How mounts fail

Failure modeWhat happens
Shear loadGravity pulls the mount down the wall, shearing bolts like scissors
Tensile loadThe load stretches the fastener — soft/inferior bolts stretch, distort, or break
Pull-outThe fastener pulls out of the wall/ceiling/structure
Shock loadingA sudden added load — an earthquake, or a person hanging on the mount

Bolts at the top of a mount carry more stress than those at the bottom; following the manufacturer's placement instructions avoids the problem. A structural engineer should review mounting plans, and a licensed engineer should sign off on any custom or modified components. If you modify another contractor's work, you become responsible for it.

Mounting specific components

Projectors have four basic orientations (front table/cart, front ceiling-inverted, rear floor, rear ceiling-inverted); use the manufacturer's throw and offset data, then set image orientation via the projector menu.

Best practice: check the mounting surface for vibration (rest your hand on it) at the time of day the system will be used with building systems running — rooftop HVAC can blur images. Screens mustn't cover alarms, thermostats, switches, or outlets; roller screens use up-limit and down-limit switches. Loudspeakers for overhead use must have enclosures designed for it.

📌 Key Term

Wall reinforcement (blocking) — fixing extra heavy timber between studs before wall finishes go on, so the wall can carry heavy displays. It requires planning and coordination among designer, installer, architect, and builder — doing it after the wall is finished means tearing it apart at extra cost. A prime example of why AV installation needs are considered before construction.

Setting Up Control Systems

Modern network-based control systems are powerful and complex — installation needs the functional design, signal-flow drawings, and IP/addressing docs, and often coordination with the programmer, designer, and IT. Every control system needs a button-by-button operational specification for each touch panel and interface. Do as much configuration and testing as possible in the workshop — troubleshooting on-site is harder and more disruptive.

Control signal types & terminations

SignalConnector / character
EthernetBidirectional; twisted-pair Cat cable on 8P8C/RJ-45, or fiber; wirelessly as Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11)
RS-232Usually DB-9; unbalanced, often bidirectional; send commands + receive feedback; configure speed/parameters per device
RS-422DB-9 or DB-25; balanced → longer distances than RS-232 via common-mode rejection
RS-485Five-pin XLR for DMX512 lighting; bidirectional balanced; up to 32 daisy-chained devices; needs 120-Ω terminations at both ends
USBBidirectional, control + AV content; Types A/B/C; v3.0+ generally not for field termination
RFMostly user interfaces; interference-prone — test on-site; uni- or bidirectional
Ramp voltageLegacy infinitely-variable analog control; no standard connector
Relays / contact closuresBinary on/off; relays execute on/off/open/close/up/down, contact closures monitor two-state status
🎯 Exam Tip

Bidirectional beats unidirectional for control because the device can confirm its status or that an action happened. This is why RS-232's two-way flow (vs. a one-way protocol) is preferred, and why the exam favors feedback-capable control.

📌 Key Term

Firmware = the control CPU's operating system (make-specific, sometimes Linux). Software = the unique application written for that specific installation, with separate programs for the controller and the touch panels/interfaces. Neither the wiring nor the hardware does anything until firmware and software are loaded. Ask the programmer about hidden pages — unseen touch-panel hot spots for configuring passwords, auto-power, and other settings.

Testing: connect the control system and controlled gear as fully as possible in the workshop and test every button against the button-by-button docs. Final on-site testing verifies cabling matches drawings, the right selection buttons appear, the right device controls appear (e.g., play/pause for a media player), each action performs its specified function, and all wall buttons, switches, and sensors work — a process that can take hours since some buttons trigger multiple or conditional actions.

Configuring Networked AV Systems

Most networked AV and control devices use TCP/IP over Ethernet and need a unique identifier — an IP address or DNS hostname. Work with the client's IT manager: submit a list of every networked device (device, manufacturer, model, MAC address, software/firmware versions, location, why it needs the network, bandwidth) and let IT assign and reserve addresses. Mark each device's setting on its back for reference. Verify connectivity by pinging the device.

Segmentation
Subnetting

Uses the IP address + subnet mask; altering the mask turns one physical network into many logical ones. Doesn't reduce bandwidth but isolates it, limiting broadcast traffic to the same subnet.

Segmentation
VLANs

Subdivide subnets — give outsiders access to (say) videoconferencing but not file servers. Independent of physical topology; a device belongs to one subnet but can be on multiple VLANs. Access control lists restrict traffic; well suited to digital signage.

Segmentation
VPNs

Secure managed links between dispersed LANs (e.g., UC systems), enabling QoS, low latency, managed routing, and multicast the open Internet can't. Cost: encryption/tunneling overhead grows packet size (risking fragmentation) and adds latency.

IP addressing schemes

SchemeHow it works
DHCPServer auto-assigns an address to each device's MAC; easy to manage, no conflicts — but a device's address can change between connections
Static IPFixed, hard-coded address (needs IP, subnet mask, device name, DNS server, gateway); required for many AV devices so control/monitoring can always find them
Reserve DHCP (hybrid)A block of static addresses set aside (by MAC) for must-not-change devices; the rest assigned dynamically — the preferred approach when a DHCP server exists
DNSMaps memorable names to IP addresses via a distributed database; many AV devices don't fully support it

Choosing Switches for AV

For AV purposes, look for switches that are:

RequirementWhy
1. ManagedA managed switch lets you create VLANs, giving you more control over the switch and network segmentation.
2. Fully Layer 3 capableRouting capabilities enable VLANs to communicate with each other, facilitating efficient data flow. These also include the IGMP function.
3. Fully nonblockingEnsures the full bandwidth of each connection regardless of how many devices communicate simultaneously. More expensive, but handles traffic more effectively.
4. Capable of IGMP version 2IGMP snooping and IGMP querier allow multicasting. IGMP acts like a referee, paying attention to what users are requesting and making data delivery more efficient.
5. PoE capableProvides power to connected devices, simplifying cabling and letting IP phones and cameras operate without separate power sources.
6. NOT "green"Avoid switches that conserve power by sleeping when not in use — for AV they may cause delays when waking up, affecting real-time audio and video.
🎯 Exam Tip

"Green" or energy-saving switching is a positive in general IT and a negative in AV. Any question contrasting general IT best practice with AV requirements is probably pointing at this, at nonblocking capacity, or at multicast handling.

Power over Ethernet Standards

IEEE PoE Standard802.3af Type 1802.3at Type 2802.3bt Type 3802.3bt Type 4
Also calledPoEPoE+4PPoEPoE
Ratified2003200920182018
Pairs used2244
Source voltage44–57 VDC50–57 VDC50–57 VDC52–57 VDC
Max current per pair350 mA600 mA600 mA877–1000 mA
Source power15.4 W30 W60 W99 W
Guaranteed power at device12.95 W24.5 W51 W73 W
Max cable loop resistance per 2 pair20 Ω12.5 Ω12.5 Ω4–12.5 Ω
Max power loss in cable2.45 W4.5 W9 W8–25 W
🎯 Exam Tip

Note the gap between source power and guaranteed power at the device — 15.4 W in, 12.95 W out for 802.3af. The difference is loss in the cable. If a question asks what a device can actually draw, the answer is the guaranteed at device figure, not the source figure.

Calculating a PoE Budget

You need to know how much power you need and whether your switch or midspan can deliver it at no more than 80% of its power rating.

  1. Find the power requirement for each piece of equipment connected to the switch — on the spec sheet or the box itself.
  2. Add all the power requirements to determine your PoE budget.
  3. Specify a switch, with enough ports, capable of providing 120% of the required budget to operate safely.
📑 Worked Example

Decoder A requires 48 V at 140 mA = 6.72 W. Encoder B requires 48 V at 185 mA = 8.88 W.
The system has 4 sources → 4 encoders: 8.88 W × 4 = 35.5 W.
The system has 12 displays → 12 decoders: 6.72 W × 12 = 80.6 W.
Total power requirement = 116.1 W, and we need 16 ports for the AV equipment.
Specify a switch delivering 120% of 116.1 W ≈ 139 W across at least 16 PoE ports.

In large PoE deployments, consider heating of cable bundles and the quality of cable used — refer to the cable manufacturer's recommendations and the NEC ampacity tables if required.

QoS: DiffServ Service Classes

One method of prioritising network traffic is categorising each traffic type into distinct QoS differentiated service (DiffServ) classes. Each class is treated differently by switches and routers, targeting different goals — one class avoids packet loss, another guarantees ordering (low jitter). The lowest-priority class is "best effort," with no guarantee of timeliness or integrity.

Service ClassPurposeLoss tol.Delay tol.Jitter tol.
SignalingControls applications or user endpoints, such as call setup/termination signalsLowLowHigh
TelephonyVoIP traffic and constant-rate transmission with minimal latencyVery lowVery lowVery low
Real-Time InteractiveInteractive apps with variable rate, requiring low jitter, loss and delayLowVery lowLow
Multimedia ConferencingConferencing that can adapt to congestion; otherwise use Real-Time InteractiveLow–mediumVery lowLow
Broadcast VideoMedia streams (live AV events, broadcast video) with low latencyVery lowMediumLow
Multimedia StreamingNon-interactive streaming media that adapts to congestion and packet lossLow–mediumMediumHigh
Low-Latency DataApplications requiring low latency and bursty data arrivalsLowLow–mediumHigh
High-Throughput DataLonger, high-volume data flows like FTP and email with moderate latencyLowMedium–highHigh
Low-Priority DataApplications tolerant of long interruptions; data of lesser importanceHighHighHigh
StandardBest-effort delivery for unassigned applications———
🎯 Exam Tip

Telephony is the only class that is "very low" across all three tolerances. Broadcast Video tolerates medium delay but almost no loss — a buffered stream can absorb latency but not dropped frames. Real-Time Interactive (think videoconference) is the opposite trade: it cannot absorb delay.

AV Networking Security Best Practices

An AV department is not divorced from the rest of the organisation's cybersecurity needs. Basic actions like changing default passwords go a long way; more advanced actions may need help from IT.

BasicAdvanced
• Change default authentication
• Disable unnecessary or harmful ports and features like Port 80 (HTTP) and Port 23 (Telnet)
• Upgrade firmware
• Integrate security into the development and planning process
• Manually vet and research devices with your security team
• Secure technology in locked racks and physically secure locations 		• Subnet your devices
• Use a dedicated IP network/VLAN segment to isolate traffic and restrict network access
• Use VLAN tagging on AV switch ports
• Enable encryption
• Include AV devices with your intrusion protection systems (IPS) and intrusion detection systems (IDS)

Producing AV Events (Temporary Systems)

Installers also set up temporary systems for presentations or performances: transport gear safely, set up and operate it, then dismantle and remove it. (Large-scale event production is beyond CTS scope.) Prepare by referencing the designs, building an equipment checklist, testing everything as safe and operational before transport, allocating crew with the right skills and licensing, planning access/parking, and building a realistic setup, testing, and rehearsal schedule.

Loading/unloading trucks: don't lift heavy/awkward items alone, bend at the knees, only licensed personnel operate forklifts/lifts, secure loads so nothing shifts toward the driver, turn road cases onto their weight-bearing side (not resting on wheels), strap items to carts, and know the truck's load limits and the law. Use dock plates/lifts/lift-gates, or ramps and forklifts if no dock; check that big items fit doorways, halls, and elevators.

📐 Spec

Throw distance = screen width × lens zoom ratio. A 3 m (10 ft) wide screen with a 2.0 lens → projector 6 m (20 ft) from the screen.

Sound-reinforcement setup: place loudspeakers to either side of the display in front of all microphones; put mics directly in front of speakers' positions and not in front of the loudspeakers (feedback); set the mixer at the room's back so you hear what the audience hears; connect everything, then power on all gear except the power amplifier — set levels, zero the amp inputs, power the amp, and bring levels up slowly. Tape down or ramp all floor cables.

Flat panels: verify airflow, use only the specified premeasured mounting bolts (wrong-length bolts can destroy the panel), lay the panel face-down on a clean blanket to attach brackets, and raise it to the mount with a partner.

Supporting AV systems

Clients often lack the in-house expertise to maintain complex systems, so vendors offer maintenance & repair (the installing company understands the system best) and system updates as needs and technology change. Ongoing support turns a one-time vendor into a long-term partner. (More in Part V.)

CHAPTER 18Operating AV Solutions

After the build: verifying the system performs to spec, briefing and training the users, handing over a complete documentation package, and keeping a maintenance log — plus striking a temporary event.

Systems Performance Verification

📌 Key Term

Commissioning → systems performance verification. Historically the AV industry called the formal testing process commissioning. But in construction, commissioning is an ongoing process spanning a building's whole life, so AVIXA renamed its narrower step systems performance verification. You'll still hear "commissioning" used by other trades — they mean the same AV step. It's a formal process of testing every element of the system to confirm it operates as intended.

📌 Key Term

ANSI/InfoComm 10:2013, "Audiovisual Systems Performance Verification" — the standard providing a framework for what to verify, when in the delivery cycle, how to set verification metrics, and how to report. It includes a reference list of ~150 verification items as a template. Its functional categories span audio, video, A/V, cable management/termination/labeling, control, electrical, IT, operations & support, physical environment, physical installation, serviceability, wireless, and documentation.

Why it matters: it gives a comprehensive step-by-step test of a complex system, lets the AV company objectively demonstrate the system meets the contracted performance specs, and catches problems to fix before handover. Verification confirms the installation is complete and ready for operation. Example: connect a display system to a test-signal generator and calibrate along the path with a test pattern, evaluating the signal at each device's input with an instrument like an oscilloscope. For networked AV, determine the network's peak load before bandwidth testing. Temporary event systems need testing too — confirm proper signal flow end to end.

Checking Signal Flow

A signal goes source → processing → destination. To verify and troubleshoot, the technician must understand how each device functions (source, processor, or destination?), how the signal flows through the system, how to correctly interconnect devices, and how to configure, adjust, and calibrate each component. In short: confirm sources generate the proper signals, signals pass through properly-functioning processors, and they reach correctly-calibrated outputs.

🎯 Exam Tip

The reason a technician learns system signal flow is to understand overall operation so they can identify the source of problems — not merely to document or to set levels. Troubleshooting is the payoff.

Support, Briefing & Training

A system succeeds only if users can actually operate it. Expect to brief clients on basics — how to start up and shut down, display images from various sources, select microphones/sources, and change volume. Briefings may be informal (a quick demo for a presenter) or part of formal training. It's best to demonstrate on the actual installed equipment.

Why comprehensive training pays off
  • Teaches end users how to use the system
  • Improves user confidence
  • Reduces service calls caused by user error
  • Reduces improper use and consequent damage
  • Enables in-house staff to do basic troubleshooting and be ready for phone support

Identify training needs during design and put requirements (duration, sessions, trainee count) in the contract. Schedule training after the system is complete and operational; train end users in small groups (up to six) for hands-on time; learn trainees' backgrounds first to pitch the material right. Consider "train the trainer" so the organization can keep training internally.

⚠ Watch Out

End-user training is not meant to eliminate the need for the AV company's maintenance and repair — that's a distractor. Training builds confidence, cuts user-error service calls, and reduces damage risk, but professional maintenance still has its place.

📐 Spec

The shutdown-order rule: where the control system doesn't manage shutdown, the user must power devices down in a specific order. For audio, shut down the power amplifier(s) first, before mixers and sources — otherwise transient noise peaks can damage the loudspeakers. A numbered checklist is the clean way to convey this.

Documentation & the Handover Package

A quick-reference guide serves typical users — how to turn the system on/off, switch program sources, mute/unmute mics, adjust volume, and use the control interface. Best practice: a single laminated A4/letter sheet (double-sided if needed) with diagrams, screenshots, large text, and simple bulleted steps, since presenters glance at it moments before using the room.

Final AV system documentation package
  • As-built drawings with field corrections — full-size and half-size paper, DWG and PDF files, reduced sheets for the racks, plus a navigation drawing for complex projects
  • Settings & adjustments schedule — signal gain, DSP/software settings, codec and projector settings, all IP and MAC addresses, phone/VoIP numbers
  • Configuration files for DSP, matrix switchers, control system, and devices (with current editing/loading software) on long-term media
  • Test reports (paper and electronic)
  • Manufacturer manuals, alphabetized, in indexed three-ring binders, plus electronic archive
  • Equipment spreadsheet — all gear with options and serial numbers
  • Custom operation guides and laminated flash-card instructions for basic operations
  • Basic troubleshooting guide (common user errors and failures)
  • Consumable spares list (lamps, filters), key schedule (three duplicates each), and recommended service intervals
  • Warranty statement — start date, terms, manufacturer coverage, extended plans

Contract-defined operational documentation may include custom user guides, as-built drawings and schedules, and manufacturer manuals. Even where not contractually required, prepare simple laminated reference materials kept with the equipment. System docs cover manuals, design/configuration and signal paths (for troubleshooting), cable schedules, DSP/switcher/software config files, control config (DIP switches, IP addresses), and end-user operating instructions in plain language.

Preventive Maintenance & Striking

Clients may contract long-term maintenance. Keep a maintenance log recording the date of each activity, who did it, problems found, corrective measures taken, and any recommended follow-up (and whether it was done). Clarity matters so any technician can quickly grasp the system's history.

Log equipment replacements (dates, signal-path or control changes) and repairs (what needs fixing, options, estimated cost, downtime).

📌 Key Term

Striking (bumping out) — removing a temporary event system; setup is bumping in. Guidelines: don't pack up until attendees have left, plan in advance, gather road cases near their gear, strike by category (all video, then all audio) or by team, coordinate space turnover and loading-dock time with in-house staff, return borrowed items to a responsible person, match gear to its labeled/bar-coded case, and leave the space as you found it (remove all tape and materials).

CHAPTER 19Managing an AV Project

The project-management chapter: breaking work down, sequencing and scheduling resources, managing the budget, coordinating with every other trade, and producing the documents that control changes.

📌 Key Term

The five project elements (all driven by the client's purpose): Scope (deliverables and activities), Time (estimation and duration), Cost (human and material resources), Quality (performance meets expectations), and Risk (threats, opportunities, responses). Many AV pros add the PMP credential (from PMI) to their CTS.

Work Breakdown Structure & Logic Network

ToolPurposeExpressed as
Work breakdown structure (WBS)First step in scoping labor; ensures everyone understands what the client will receive; breaks work into manageable pieces, each descending level more detailed; a baseline for estimates and change management. Does not address who, when, what, or how much.nouns (a product/service)
Logic network diagramSequences and schedules activities and milestones; lists activities and their sequential relationships, identifies dependencies, predecessors, and successors; activities enter by dependency, not time constraintverbs (build, test, fabricate, develop)
📌 Key Term

Milestones — key project events (a major deliverable done, an important event), often tied to scheduled payments or client approvals. Examples: materials delivered, racks programmed, projectors calibrated. Shown as diamonds or triangles on the logic network. Each activity should have an associated deliverable.

📌 Key Term

Effort vs. Duration. Effort is the total work time a task takes in its entirety. Duration is how long it will actually take — effort plus resource availability, number of available resources, and calendars (weekends/holidays). "Perfect-world" (best-case) estimating of effort is optimistic and raises risk of underbidding labor; mature organizations check resources across all current projects first.

Budget & Site Monitoring

📌 Key Term

Price ≠ cost. The client's price = the company's cost (labor, supplies, equipment) + a markup covering overhead (taxes, rent, insurance, benefits) and profit. The project budget is the labor, supplies, and equipment the company estimates are needed to complete the agreed work — i.e., what the PM allocates, not what the client paid and not what ends up being spent.

The PM manages how resources are spent so actual cost stays within the allocation, tracks staff activity against the contract's quality standards, and investigates overruns to get back on track. Any change to site conditions or client requests that affects the budget must be explicitly agreed by both parties. On-site monitoring objectives: work is safe and code-compliant, meets company quality standards, conforms to the contract, stays on schedule, and any problems or conflicts are addressed.

Coordination, Kickoff & Status Meetings

An AV install is often part of a larger construction effort. Stakeholders to coordinate with include the general contractor, and the lighting, AV, data/telecom, IT, mechanical, security, electrical, life-safety, plumbing, and structural contractors. The GC and/or construction manager usually coordinate the trades; conflicts caught before work starts are easiest to resolve, so communication is critical. Live-event projects add stakeholders like the promoter, production and stage management, set/costume/lighting/audio designers, rigging and effects, unions, safety, broadcast, and the talent.

Meeting
Kickoff meeting

Held before work begins so teams get acquainted and set communication rules. Presided over by the owner's PM, construction manager, or GC. Establishes protocols — forms, financial/design authorizations, payment process, RFI handling, lines of communication — that stay consistent all project. Also covers sequencing, owner politics, contract/billing issues, delivery/storage/security logistics, and "clean and clear dates" for installing in finished spaces.

Meeting
Weekly status meetings

Each team's PM reports progress and cross-team issues; schedules update and conflicts resolve. AV providers may skip early meetings but should visit as their rooms get built. The organizer keeps and distributes minutes with action items.

The Six Project Meeting Types

Regular meetings serve different purposes across the life of the project, and they run in this order:

#MeetingPurpose
1ProgrammingHeld to understand the client's goals and level of technical sophistication
2Design coordinationHeld at major project milestones to review design progress with the client and coordinate with the rest of the design team
3Pre-bidHeld with the client and potential contractors to review project scope where bidding is required
4Pre-constructionHeld with the client and potential contractors to review the scope of the project
5ConstructionHeld during construction to observe progress and address issues on-site
6Post-constructionHeld with the client to review the project
📌 Key Term

Meeting minutes from each project meeting should include: date and location; purpose of the meeting; an agenda; attendees and their respective roles (job titles, who they represent); items discussed and resolved; and action items.

Coordination meetings are scheduled with these professionals throughout all phases of the project: building architect, interior designer, AV professional, IT consultants, acoustical consultant, lighting designer, and structural, mechanical and electrical systems engineers.

The process should include programming meetings during pre-design and schematic design; design coordination meetings throughout design development and construction document phases; and design review meetings with stakeholders. The purpose, frequency, duration and location of each meeting should be predetermined.

How the Standards Line Up

Three standards describe the same project from different angles. Being able to map a phase in one onto a phase in another is a favourite exam move:

StandardIts stages
ISO 21500:2012
Guidance on project management process groups		Initiating → Planning → Implementing → Controlling → Closing
ANSI/INFOCOMM 2M-2010
Standard Guide for AV Design and Coordination Processes		Program Phase → Design Phase → Construction Phase
INFOCOMM 10:2013
Audiovisual Systems Performance Verification		Spans the Construction Phase
🎯 Exam Tip

Memorise the three standard numbers and what each governs: 2M-2010 = design and coordination process, 10:2013 = performance verification, ISO 21500 = generic project management. Note that performance verification sits inside Construction — it is not a separate phase after handover.

Schedules & Sequencing AV with Other Trades

📌 Key Term

Gantt chart — the most common project-schedule format: tasks and subtasks as horizontal bars on a timeline, showing sequence, milestones, and dependencies (tasks that can't start until others finish — e.g., walls must be finished and painted before fragile AV components are mounted).

🎯 Exam Tip

The defining trait of AV installation vs. other trades: the bulk of the AV system — the electronics — must go in after all other trades finish and the site is clean, because the equipment is so sensitive to dust, moisture, and temperature. But note the sequencing subtlety: raceways/conduit/backboxes go in first, cable is pulled before the ceiling grid closes, and the electronics come last.

Many construction aspects affect AV: millwork built to tolerance, correctly sized/located conduit and power, lighting zones checked against images and cameras, HVAC ductwork monitored for conflicts, loading docks/elevators/doorways big enough for large screens and racks, existing-facility use (noise, delivery hours), ceiling layout coordinated with ceiling-mounted AV, acoustic treatments reviewed, hazardous work (welding, painting, concrete, sanding) finished before equipment arrives, and data/telecom activated before functional testing.

Project Documentation

Decisions and changes must be documented, signed or verifiably approved by all relevant parties, and often become part of the contracts. Every document should carry project-specific references (owner name/address, install locations, contractor names, project numbers).

DocumentPurpose
Letter of transmittalFormal cover letter sent with any documents/drawings/samples — lists what's enclosed and any action required
Request for information (RFI)Formally asks a question about the project — a design issue, a site issue, or an owner change/request; may resolve with a clarification or escalate to a contract change
Progress reportReports completion status as of a date, flagging anything affecting schedule or budget
Request for change (RFC)Proposes changing contractual obligations, equipment models, specs, or design — must include pricing and project impact; any team member can submit, commonly the integrator/consultant; an approved RFC becomes a change order
Change order (CO)Documents agreed-upon changes to specs/contract as the project progresses — arguably the most important construction-phase form since it changes scope and pricing; approvers set by contract; notify guarantors if it pushes value past budget
Construction change directive (CCD) / field orderIssued for time-critical field conditions to trigger immediate work, bypassing the formal RFI–RFC–CO process; used by owner or GC
🎯 Exam Tip

Two frequently tested flows: when a building-design change affects the AV install, the AV vendor submits an RFC; and when a client requests a change that raises cost, the correct response is a change order (CO) signed by both parties — not silently absorbing the work or refusing outright.

PART IV📋 Summary

The Part IV storyline
  • Ch 17 — Integrating: Prepare and inspect gear before installing; terminate cable expertly (poor terminations are the #1 problem — test with a continuity check); know the methods (direct/compression/solder/crimp/linear-compression/IDC) and connectors (XLR, RCA, ¼", ⅛", BNC, RJ-45); build racks with good ergonomics, weight at the bottom, forward-facing RF antennas, and one of three cooling methods (convection/evacuation/forced air) plus signal separation; pull cable through the right conduit (pull box every 30 m/100 ft or 180° of bend; fill 53%/31%/40% for 1/2/3 cables; bend radius ≥4× diameter; cross at 90°; keep mic cables separate); mount to a 5× safety factor (know shear/tensile/pull-out/shock failures and blocking); wire and configure control systems (RS-232/422/485, bidirectional preferred, firmware vs software, button-by-button spec); configure networked AV (subnets, VLANs, VPNs, DHCP/static/reserve-DHCP/DNS); and set up temporary events (throw = width × zoom ratio; power the amp on last).
  • Ch 18 — Operating: Verify performance (AVIXA renamed commissioning to "systems performance verification"; ANSI/InfoComm 10:2013, ~150 items); learn signal flow to troubleshoot; brief and train users (small groups ≤6, after the system is complete, train-the-trainer); power down in a specific order (amps first for audio); hand over the full documentation package (as-builts, settings schedules, config files, manuals, warranty); keep a maintenance log; and strike temporary events cleanly.
  • Ch 19 — Managing: Balance the five elements (scope, time, cost, quality, risk); build a WBS (nouns, deliverables) and logic network (verbs, sequencing, dependencies, milestones); distinguish effort from duration; remember price ≠ cost and the budget is what's allocated; coordinate every trade through kickoff and weekly status meetings; schedule with Gantt charts respecting dependencies (AV electronics go in last, on a clean site); and control changes with the right document (letter of transmittal, RFI, progress report, RFC, CO, CCD).
🎯 Exam Tip

Part IV's most-tested numbers & rules: conduit fill 53% / 31% / 40% (1/2/3 cables) · pull box every 30 m (100 ft) or 180° of bend · bend radius ≥4× diameter · cross cables at 90° · mounting safety factor ×5 · accessible controls 380–1,220 mm (15–48 in) AFF · RS-485 up to 32 devices, 120 Ω terminations · train in groups of ≤6 · amps off first · throw = width × zoom ratio · standard ANSI/InfoComm 10:2013.
